Abstract
This study addresses the paradoxical problem of the advocacy for ‘namelessness’
in Daoist philosophy and the myriad of name-empowered phenomena in Daoist
religion. Its particular focus is on the functions of names in three rituals from the
early Way of Celestial Masters (142–fourth century ce): the exorcism of demons
the ordination of priests
column2: and the summoning of divinities in healing rituals.

column1: The study takes an analytical approach upon the above cases. It has been
found that the application of names in these rituals has an ordering effect upon
the Daoist community in three respects: religiously
column2: name-empowered rituals

column1: invoke effective channels of communication with the bureaucratic institutions
which govern the realms of the Celestial
column2: Terrestrial

column1: they provide concrete means for Daoists to deal with real life problems that
are beyond the control of common people; and politically
column2: they contribute to

column1: the organisation of a hierarchical monastic system
column2: which maintains the Daoist

column1: values
column2: beliefs
column5: and taboos. The efficacy of those rituals is

column1: achieved by a trade-off between the commitment to Daoist belief and the divine
powers that provide ready solutions to human sufferings

column1: possession. Thus
column2: they serve as divine interventions in times of disrupted order.

column1: This connotation of names provides a solution to the paradox which lies
at the heart of this thesis: the philosophical state of the namelessness can be
